title: SP-VLA: Joint Model Scheduling and Token Pruning for Robotic Speed
one_liner: A robot thinks fast when the next action is routine, and slow when it truly needs to decide.
lead: Vision-Language-Action models let robots understand images and generate the right physical movements. But they run slowly, sending every image through the full model every time, which is too sluggish for real-world robotic tasks. SP-VLA accelerates these models by routing simple, repetitive actions through a lightweight fast-pass, while routing tricky decisions through the full model. It also removes redundant visual data that does not matter for the current action.

paras: A robot that sees and acts must first convert each camera image into numbers, then run those numbers through a big model to generate the next movement command. This takes time, maybe half a second or more per image. Real robots picking objects or navigating need to react faster, roughly every 50 milliseconds, because objects move and hands need frequent updates. Running the full model every time burns so much compute the robot misses these deadlines.

A simple fix would be to use a smaller, faster model instead. But smaller models have less understanding of the image and scene, so they produce jerky or unsafe actions. The robot trades speed for accuracy, and with lives at stake, neither outcome is acceptable.

callout.html: Route easy actions through a fast, lightweight model and hard actions through the full model.

panels.title: 1. The setup
panels.caption: A robot sees an image and needs to move. Every pixel matters for safety.

panels.title: 2. The problem
panels.caption: Full model runs every frame. Compute per action stays constant, too slow.

panels.title: 3. The insight
panels.caption: Some actions need full thought; others are just habit.

panels.title: 4. The method
panels.caption: Deliberative: full model and important pixels. Intuitive: lightweight model, fewer pixels.

panels.title: 5. The payoff
panels.caption: Latency halves. Accuracy stays high or improves on realistic robot tasks.

steps.text: Predict: is this movement routine or does it need full analysis?
Send to lightweight model; trim redundant image pixels first.
Send full image and full model for complex decisions.
Strip away pixels that do not affect this specific action.
Combine outputs and send motor commands.

paras: The paper changes two things: which model runs for each action, and which parts of the image the model sees.

hidden.name: whether an action needs full reasoning
paras: The paper measures a hidden property of each action: how much thinking does this movement need? Routine actions like continuing to grip an object require less. Risky actions like approaching a new part of the scene require more thought.

The paper learns this by training a small network (a classifier) that looks at the image and the last few past actions to predict: deliberative or intuitive. When running the robot later (after training finishes), the predictions guide which path each action takes through the system.

heat.caption: Darker means harder decisions; lighter means routine. Boxes show where the classifier marks hard moments.

reads.html: Humans do this intuitively. When picking up a familiar object, your hand moves on autopilot. When reaching for something fragile or in a tight space, you slow down and think carefully.

The paper trains a small network on task demonstrations to assign each action a score or label: hard or routine. When the robot runs later, high-difficulty actions go to the full model; low-difficulty actions go to a lightweight generator, which runs faster because it has fewer layers and parameters to process, meaning fewer arithmetic operations per action.

paras: The core insight is that robot actions in a sequence are not independent. Many steps in a task are repetitive or follow a pattern. A robot gripping an object does not need to reanalyze the full scene every 10 milliseconds; it can execute the grip routine on intuition. Only when something changes—a new object appears, the grip fails, navigation starts—does the robot need the full model.

By routing routine actions through a lightweight model, the system cuts compute by 40 to 60 percent while keeping the same latency for hard decisions, because the lightweight model runs faster and still produces safe actions for well-learned patterns. The pruning of image data removes visual noise: if this action is about continuing to grip, the system does not need to analyze distant walls or irrelevant objects. Fewer pieces of image data mean faster processing because the model has fewer numbers to read and think about, and it stays focused on what matters.

stages.s: if routine: prune image, send to lightweight model
if hard: send full image to full model

math.words: latency equals the sum of classification time plus model time plus pruning time, weighted by how often each path is taken
math.equation: L_total = w_routine * L_lightweight + w_deliberative * L_full + L_classify + L_prune
symbols: fraction of actions classified as routine
time to run action classifier (fixed, small)
time to prune image tokens (proportional to pruning rate)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose 70% of actions are routine, 30% hard.
Lightweight model runs in 15 ms; full model in 50 ms.
Classification takes 2 ms; pruning takes 1 ms.

math.note: The faster a lightweight model is, and the higher the fraction of routine actions, the bigger the speedup, because you replace slow operations with fast ones more often.

charts.title: Full model always
charts.note: Accurate but slow, misses real-time deadlines.

charts.title: SP-VLA (this paper)
charts.note: Faster because we replace full-model compute with lightweight-model compute on 70% of actions. More accurate because the classifier learned to send hard actions to the full model, so the full model can focus entirely on the tricky decisions.

items.html: If the classifier wrongly calls a hard action routine, the lightweight model produces a poor movement and the robot fails. The fix is careful training of the classifier on many different task demonstrations.

If important visual details are removed, the model loses context. Example: if the system strips away pixels showing a nearby obstacle while the robot is navigating, the lightweight model cannot see it and might bump into it.
If the robot encounters a task or environment very different from training, the classifier may mislabel actions, breaking both the speedup and safety, because the patterns it learned no longer apply.

The action classifier must work well when scene and lighting change slightly. Pruning rules must always keep image data for places where the robot could collide or fail. Lightweight model must actually run fast with no hidden delays.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple robotic task: a simulated arm that moves between three goal positions in sequence. Train the action classifier on 100 demonstrations. Measure: (1) latency per action on the lightweight path versus the full path, (2) success rate on a held-out test sequence, (3) the speedup ratio (time without routing divided by time with routing).
demo.closing: If the demo runs without the routing logic, the speedup should be close to 1 (no benefit). If routing is active and the classifier is trained, speedup should exceed 1.3-fold with the same success rate.
